newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed takes aim at Russian budget in power stuggle.
newsitem.headline: Lebed takes aim at Russian budget in power stuggle.

text.p: Russian security tsar Alexander Lebed blasted the government's budget plans in remarks published on Friday, adding a new twist to Kremlin infighting as President Boris Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery.

The daily newspaper Izvestia published extracts of a letter sent by Lebed to Yeltsin on August 29 seeking radical changes in the 1997 budget planned by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. A copy of the letter was later obtained by Reuters.

Izvestia said Lebed had also criticised government spending plans in a letter to Chernomyrdin, but his written comments to Yeltsin were a further sign of jostling for position by two men who could become presidential rivals.

"Alexander Lebed is behaving as if early presidential elections have already been called," the newspaper commented in a front-page article under the banner headline "General Launches Attack on Budget".

Speculation over a power struggle grew over the summer after Yeltsin remained out of the Kremlin on vacation following his re-election on July 3. He announced last week that he planned to have surgery, described by experts as a heart bypass operation.
Lebed and Chernomyrdin would be among possible successors if Yeltsin proved unfit to rule and a new election was called.

Lebed, who has no direct responsibility for economic matters in his security brief, attacked what he called the underfunding of the military and other sectors ranging from agriculture to industry, high technology, science, culture and education.
"This dooms the whole 1997 budget sphere of the majority of enterprises to even more financial problems next year," the 46-year-old former paratroop general wrote.

He proposed raising revenue by increasing prices for natural resources, ending foreign firms' preferential import duties, putting export duties on gas and charging higher rents for the use of state property.
"We suggest that it is advisable to charge the government of the Russian Federation to substantially revise its forecast and the 1997 budget bill," he said.
Lebed, who favours a strong centralised government but espouses a free market, justified his intervention by portraying the alleged underfunding as a threat to national security.

He made several statements about the economy soon after he was appointed Yeltsin's national security adviser and Security Council secretary last June following his success in coming third in the first round of the presidential election.
Chernomyrdin quickly made clear at the time that the economy was his own sphere and went beyond Lebed's brief.
Although both men meet regularly, Chernomyrdin has distanced himself from Lebed and criticised some aspects of the peace deal he negotiated last month to end fighting in Chechnya.
The power struggle also involves Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais who is widely seen as keen to consolidate his own position, although he is unlikely to run for president.

"This (letter) is part of the power struggle involving Lebed, Chernomyrdin and Chubais but there is another level -- the horrible state of the economy," political analyst Viktor Kremenyuk told Reuters.

"If the economic situation does not change for the better quickly, there could be crises in some areas which put the security of the state in question. In this respect, Lebed has every reason to raise the alarm."
